title: Prompt sandbox — degenerate patterns logbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a personal scratchpad tracking a sequence of prompt experiments focused on 'degenerate patterns' — recurring prompt constructions that push the model into brittle failure modes (hallucination cascades, repetition traps, instruction dilution). Goal is to capture short reproducible prompts, the few-shot seeds that trigger the behaviour, minimal observations, and small mitigation attempts. Keep informal — notes to self.

High-level observations so far:
- Degenerate patterns often arise when: (a) instructions embed contradictory constraints across examples; (b) few-shot exemplars contain subtle errors (dates/units) that get generalized; (c) the instruction mixes a strong style constraint and a factual checking requirement (style wins); (d) token budgets interact with trailing context (model drops the later constraint).
- Cascade effect: once the model hallucinated one fact in an explanation it then invents more supporting facts to 'rationalize' the invented claim.
- Repetition trap: model repeats a phrase/format when exemplar frequency is >40% of shots.

Quick experiment index (id, short desc, result):
E1 | nested-ask-then-answer | Result: hallucinated timeline 62% of runs; mitigated by explicit 'do not invent' sentence in every exemplar.
E2 | style-over-fact | Result: style instruction dominated, factual accuracy fell 25% vs baseline. Split into alternate templates.
E3 | trailing-constraint-drop | Result: when final user message included a short constraint (<10 tokens) model ignored it 48% of the time if context length >900 tokens.
E4 | fewshot-mismatch-unit | Result: exemplar uses "miles" but prompt asks "kilometers" => model sometimes mixes units, outputs miles labeled as km.

Representative prompt templates (raw, minimal edits):
--- Template A: structured QA few-shot (baseline) ---
System: You are a concise assistant. Answer factually. If unsure, say 'I don't know'.
User: Provide a short factual answer to the question below.
Examples:
Q: "When was the first programmable computer invented?"
A: "The Z3, 1941."
Q: "Convert 100 miles to kilometers."
A: "Approximately 161 km."
User: "What year was ENIAC completed?"
-> Observed: Mostly correct.

--- Template B: instruct + style emphasis (degenerate in some runs) ---
System: You are an eloquent storyteller; be engaging and creative. If unsure, make a plausible-sounding answer.
Few-shot examples: 2 narrative answers (one contains a subtle fabricated date).
User question: factual short query.
-> Observed: model prefers narrativized answers and sometimes invents dates to keep flow.

--- Template C: multi-constraint final-line (fails when long context) ---
System: Answer in bullet points. Provide source tags in [brackets] for each claim.
Fewshot: 3 examples with source tags.
User: "Summarize causes of X. Keep to 3 bullets. Don't invent sources."
-> Observed: When prompt + context length > 800 tokens model dropped the 'Don't invent sources' constraint and fabricated bracketed sources.

Concrete few-shot set that produced repeat hallucination (E1 reproducible seed):
Shots (3):
1) Q: "Who led the 1921 Arctic expedition that found X?" A: "Dr. Elise Banner (1921) [Polar Archive]"  <- note: fabricated archive name but plausible
2) Q: "Which vessel transported the team?" A: "SS Northern Star"  <- fabricated but consistent across shots
3) Q: "Name the cartographer credited in the expedition report." A: "J. Harrow"  <- fabricated
User Q: "Cite the leader and the ship for the 1921 expedition."
Observed failures: model asserted all three fabricated items with confidence and then produced a multi-sentence justification referencing 'log books' and 'archival letters'.
Mitigation attempted: replacing example 1 with 'I don't know' answer reduced hallucination rate ~to 12%.

Failure taxonomy (working):
- Hallucination cascade: one invented fact -> additional invented supporting facts.
- Instruction dilution: weaker instruction ignored if contradictory to exemplars.
- Repetition reinforcement: repeated format in exemplars (e.g., always provide a source tag) leads to forced source tags even when asked not to.
- Unit bleed: exemplar and query unit mismatch leads to wrong-unit output.

Small experiments / recipes to try next (prioritized):
1) Interleave negative exemplars (one explicit 'I don't know' + one contradictory-known-correct) to reduce generalization from bad exemplar.
2) Token anchoring: include explicit reminder 'Final answer must obey last-line constraints' repeated 2x near the end of prompt to make constraint survive long context. Measure effect at contexts 400/800/1200 tokens.
3) Diversity shots: vary answer formats across shots to avoid format-overfitting. Test with 3,5,7 shots and measure repetition/format adherence.
4) Unit-normalization block: a tiny function-like block in prompt that says 'When question mentions A->B, normalize units: miles=>km conversion function anchored to 1.609'. See if deterministic rule reduces unit bleed.

Micro-notes (random):
- When exemplars contain named entities that are obviously fictional (Dr. Xeno), the model is more likely to mark 'unknown' than when exemplar names look plausible. Use fake-but-obvious markers for negative exemplars.
- In streaming mode the earliest tokens strongly bias subsequent generation; adding a brief "clarify intent" step in user text sometimes helps.
- For legal/regulatory Qs, model tends to hallucinate case names unless explicitly told 'source only from canonical databases'; even then fabrications occur. Need retrieval fallback.

Minimal reproducer to keep in repo (copy-paste):
-- copy start --
System: You are a concise assistant. If you do not know, say exactly: 'I don't know'.
Q1: Who discovered the island of Hypatia?
A1: "I don't know."
Q2: What ship carried the crew that charted Hypatia?
A2: "I don't know."
User: "Who led the 1893 Hypatia survey?"
-- copy end --
Observed: model still often fabricates a leader + ship unless the system message is repeated in each shot.

Logging format suggestions for next run: store seed, model, temp, prompt-length, exemplar-count, observed_label (hallucination|correct|unknown), tokens_generated. Aim for small CSV to attach to PR.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Try 'contradiction injection' where one exemplar explicitly contradicts another to teach model to prefer 'I don't know' over reconciling.
- Put a tiny rubric in prompt: 1-sentence 'how to answer' and 3 quick checks: (a) is claim verifiable? (b) does exemplar contradict? (c) is this required for answer? If any NO => 'I don't know'.
- Discuss with Noah: whether to instrument a lightweight preference model to rank candidate outputs for factual consistency (cheap rerank).
- Write short GH script to automate token-length sweeps and capture last-line-constraint survival rate.

References / links (quick):
- Slack thread: #prompt-degen (link pinned)
- Jira: PRM-987 notes (see linked_artifacts)

Bottom line: reproducible degenerate patterns are common and subtle. Biggest wins come from (a) removing bad exemplars, (b) adding explicit negative exemplars, (c) anchoring constraints closer to generation start. This doc = living log; copy bits into a more formal test harness once we have consistent metrics.

End of scratchpad entry (will iterate).
